about: What a small ship's crew say to each other out in the dark (src/carrier/deep.mjs): the quiet between orders, how far from home she is, and what the deep throws at them. Said only aboard a ship whose crew are named here (the cutter), while she is out of her berth, with no raid on. Each entry is a short exchange: `say` is [who, words] in turn. `when` is what lets it be said: `quiet` (out, nothing happening), `far` (over 3 km from home), `deep` (the deep factor over 0.75, about 5 km), `home` (back inside 1.5 km after being out past 3 km), and the deep's events: `debris` (a wreck fragment in sight), `drive` and `drive-out` (a far drive seen, then gone dark), `ghost` and `ghost-gone` (a return on the plot that comes to nothing), `ping` (grit on the hull), `radio` (flight control breaking up with range). Each entry is said once per page; an event with all its entries said says nothing.

say: Listen to her. Pumps, fans, the reactor. That is a happy ship.
Nothing out there to hit, and I still watch the scope like there is.
Drink some water. Out here you forget to.
Twenty-one degrees in here. Minus a hundred and forty on the shaded plating. Half a metre of us in between.
She will be there. Eyes on your screens.
Every time we come out I do the sums. Air for sixty days. Water for ninety. Nobody for a long way.
This far out, nobody is coming in ten minutes. If anything happens, we are the help. Remember that.
Turn the panel lights down sometime. You stop seeing the stars and start seeing how many there are.
My first trip out I checked the hull readings every ten seconds. As if it would help.
This. For a very long way.
You can't tell we're moving. Look at it. We could be doing a thousand. We could be stopped.
We are doing what the screen says.
Home's lit. Let us not keep her waiting.
Her strobe in sight. I always breathe out a little, there.
That's plating. Hull plate and a frame. Somebody's ship.
Something off the bow. No lights.
Old wreck. They drift for a hundred years.
Log the bearing and keep clear.
Drive flare, way out. Not one of ours.
Too far to matter. Log it.
She's cut her drive. Gone dark.
Then she does not want to be seen. Keep watching.
Return on the plot. Long way out. No transponder.
Ice. A rock. The set chasing its own tail.
Hull's fine. A grain of sand, faster than a bullet. It leaves a pit you could lose a fingernail in.
That one was close to the tanks.
On a ship this size, everything is close to something.
Flight control is breaking up. We are a long way out.
